name: Fair Lending and Bias Testing
title: Fair Lending and Bias Testing
answer: Fair lending and bias testing covers how lenders and credit decision systems evaluate applicants without unlawful disparate treatment or disparate impact on protected characteristics such as race, national origin, sex, marital status, age, or receipt of public assistance. It applies to mortgage, auto, small business, credit card, and other consumer credit products. The field includes statistical tests for underwriting, pricing, redlining, steering, and servicing outcomes. It also covers model risk management for artificial intelligence and machine learning models used in credit decisions.

sections.body: Fair lending and bias testing covers how lenders and credit decision systems evaluate applicants without unlawful disparate treatment or disparate impact on protected characteristics such as race, national origin, sex, marital status, age, or receipt of public assistance. It applies to mortgage, auto, small business, credit card, and other consumer credit products. The field includes statistical tests for underwriting, pricing, redlining, steering, and servicing outcomes. It also covers model risk management for artificial intelligence and machine learning models used in credit decisions.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Fair lending testing runs on loan-level data sets that combine application, underwriting, pricing, and performance records with demographic data from the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act, the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, or matched proxies such as the Bayesian Improved Surname Geocoding method. The work uses statistical software such as R, Python, and SAS, along with specialized fair lending libraries and internal model validation platforms. Cloud data warehouses and secure enclaves hold sensitive applicant data.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Analysts compare approval rates, denial reasons, interest rates, fees, and loan outcomes across protected class and control groups. They use regression models with controls for legitimate underwriting factors, and they compute disparity ratios, marginal effects, and residual differences. For machine learning models, they run pre-deployment and post-deployment tests for group fairness metrics such as demographic parity, equalized odds, and calibration by group. They also review model inputs for proxies of protected class and conduct less discriminatory alternative searches.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Fair lending is enforced by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the Department of Justice, the Federal Reserve, the FDIC, the OCC, and state attorneys general under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, the Fair Housing Act, and the Community Reinvestment Act. Lenders face examination findings, enforcement actions, private litigation, and reputational harm when models produce disparate impact without a legitimate business necessity. The site's 210 compliance and regulation pages include fair lending examination procedures and enforcement orders. Model documentation must show data provenance, feature selection, and testing results to satisfy examiners.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Regulators are increasing scrutiny of artificial intelligence and machine learning underwriting models, including generative AI used in credit decisioning and chatbots. Fair lending testing is moving toward continuous monitoring and automated bias detection rather than point-in-time model validation. The use of alternative data, such as cash flow and rental payment history, raises new questions about proxy variables and explainability. There is also growing attention to algorithmic fairness in small business lending and in pricing models that set individualized rates.
